utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today I'm glad to greet all the people present here, the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, as well as the accused, and also all the people helping us in the courtroom. First of all, I am going to read out an oral decision. Thereafter, I'll give the floor to Mr. Scott, who has something to say regarding changes within the OTP. Oral decision regarding documents introduced through the testimony of Mr. Herbert Okun. The witness appeared before the Trial Chamber from the 2nd to the 5th of April, 2007. During his testimony, he was shown a certain number of documents by the parties, and some were mere excerpts. Following the testimony of the witness, the parties submitted their IC lists of exhibits they wanted to tender into evidence. To date, in spite of the request made by the Trial Chamber through the court deputy, the Prosecution has yet to identify the excerpts presented to the witness and to be tendered into evidence. The Trial Chamber wants to recall that following the guideline number 4 attached to the decision on the admission of evidence of 13th of July, 2006, when a party submits only an excerpt of a document at the hearing it may only ask for that excerpt to be tendered into evidence, and it is under the obligation of conveying to a Chamber the numbers of -- or the page numbers or paragraph that correspond to the excerpts. Once again, the Trial Chamber invites the Prosecution to file a new IC list specifying the page numbers or the numbers of the pages presented to Witness Herbert Okun at the hearing and that the Prosecution wants to seek to tender into evidence. The Trial Chamber reminds the Prosecution that it will be able to seek to tender document that would not have been presented to the witness during the hearing through another witness or by way of a written motion pursuant to guideline number 6 of the 29th of November, 2006 decision. So in a nutshell, the Prosecution will have to submit a new IC list with regard to the excerpts presented to the witness. If the Prosecution plans to seek to tender other excerpts that have not been submitted to the witness, it will be able to do so through another witness or else file a written motion seeking admission under or pursuant to guideline number 6 of the decision of the 29th of November, 2006. So this was the oral decision. You have the floor, Mr. Scott, because I believe there's a change within the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. President, Your Honours, good afternoon; and good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Before I turn to that matter, I just will say I appreciate the Court's further guidance on the matter of the Okun exhibits. This was a situation in which there was some agreement -- both agreement and disagreement with the Prlic team because I believe it was their position that they asked or had hoped that all of the diaries would come in. The Prosecution share that same position although we disagreed on other aspects of the submission. So I do appreciate nonetheless the Chamber's additional guidance and we will make -- we will follow our new IC listing in the next day or two. I thank the Chamber for that. Your Honour, I come to the Chamber this afternoon with somewhat -- well, mixed emotions, because I have to advise the Chamber and to all those in the courtroom that our Prosecution team is losing -- will be losing in the next several weeks a member who I believe has been of great assistance both to me personally and to -- I hope to the Chamber and to the -- and to the case in general. All of you know that Mr. Mundis has been my right-hand man or colleague or co-equals here in this case, and has done a great job in my view in terms of the contribution he's made to the case. However, all along the way he has been the senior trial attorney assigned to the Delic case and given changes, which sometimes happen from time to time in this institution in terms of scheduling, the trial of the Delic case has been moved up to probably start relatively soon. Not -- an exact date has not been set, but sometime fairly soon, which, of course, unfortunately, certainly for me and I think for all of us, it's unfortunate that Mr. Mundis will not be able to continue with us. But he isn't gone yet. I think you will still be seeing him in the courtroom for a bit longer. But today seemed like the best time to begin to make the transition for a number of reasons. Having said all that, that's the bad news, and at least again from my perspective the good news is that Mr. Douglas Stringer is joining the team and is also with us today, and Douglas, you might just stand up so everyone can see who you are. Unfortunately Judge Trechsel is probably behind the pole.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, if the Court would allow me, Mr. Stringer has been practising law since 1984, so he has substantial years in the practice of law. He has been both a Prosecutor and a Defence attorney. As a Prosecutor he worked at the US Department of Justice from 1985 to 1989. Then he served very well here at the OTP from 1997 to 2002. During that time he worked very closely on the Blaskic case and on the so-called Tuta-Stela or Naletilic-Martinovic case. He therefore does bring with him extensive background in what we might call the Bosnian Croat cases. And as the Chamber knows, there is some similarity or relation between the Tuta-Stela case in particular and this case. So unfortunately for the team, and for the Prosecution team and for me, if there's one person who might be able to step into in some way the shoes of Mr. Mundis and come in from outside the institution with some relevant background and training and experience, it's certainly Mr. Stringer, and so I'm happy to have him coming on board with us. Just another couple of seconds about his background. He served very well in a number of international positions. He was an international prosecutor with the United Nations Mission in Kosovo, UNMIK, in 2004, so he has served in that capacity. During 2005 he was an international lawyer working in Sarajevo on the newly created Special Chamber or State Court for War Crimes. So the Chamber can see he brings a diverse and rich set of experiences to his time on this team. During other parts of his career, including most recently, he has practiced in the area of criminal defence, including especially black collar crime, so he does bring both prosecution and defence experience to the Prosecution team. So I thank you, Your Honour and Mr. President, for allowing me to introduce him today, and again he will be making the transition into the team over the next weeks and probably won't be here every day but he and Mr. Mundis will be both making -- both making the transition in and out of the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott. On behalf of my colleagues, I wish you welcome, Mr. Stringer. You're going to help Mr. Scott in the next few months, and I wish you welcome. Let me use this opportunity to tell you, Mr. Mundis, how sad we are to see you go. We know you are being called to work in another trial, in the Delic case, and given the resources in the OTP, we -- you have to find a substitute for you, Mr. Mundis, and this is why you're leaving us. We've known you for a year now on this case. I personally have known you for over three years, since you were representing the OTP in the other trial presided over, Hadzihasanovic and Kubura. And, Mr. Mundis, you always provable to be a very convivial man, always a smile on your face, and you were very useful on our on-site visit. So I want to pay tribute to you, wish you good luck within your next mission in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we be associated with what Your Honour has said. We will regards Mr. Mundis as a great loss to the trial. His -- I think his willingness to assist everyone, his sense of fairness have been very obvious to all of us and we wish him the best in his new endeavours and, who knows, he may be back before the trial ends. We also join in welcoming Mr. Stringer on board, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I just wish to add thank you very much. We can now move on so this incident isn't the cause for complaints of loss of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have a witness. Before speaking about the time the witness will take, I'm going to give the court deputy the floor because he's still in position just as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through which is Lizde Alija. The list submitted by the open shall be given Exhibit number IC 531. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 532. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 533. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 534. And finally, the list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit number IC 535. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. With regard to the next witness the OTP scheduled six hours. The Defence teams will also have six hours. There are six accused. Therefore, that is an hour for each accused, but they, if they so wish, split that differently. So this is how we're going to go about this hearing. This testimony should take four days. Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we have the witness, I indicated to the registrar that I wanted to make two very brief oral submissions. One is in regard to -- on last Wednesday there was an observation made from the Bench, actually a ruling, I should say, that one federal rules of evidence may be applying, that is Rule 611. Some of us are familiar with that rule. And based on that, I guess I would like to know what other rules of evidence from the US federal rules of evidence are being applied in this Tribunal or if all of them; if not, some of them. If other rules of evidence are being applied from other jurisdictions, I would like to know as well, because, and this is where I guess the crux of my concern is, Judge Trechsel indicated that answers to leading questions are of little value, and over the past few days I've been thinking about that, and I'm extremely concerned. As you might recall, I even give -- gave Judge Trechsel the -- the opportunity to perhaps correct himself, but if that is the case, that means that all leading questions for the last year that have been posed by counsel for the Defence, as they are entitled to under the rules, have little value. The answers, that is, from those leading questions. And this seems to be a new rule, a rule that I wasn't aware of. My colleagues aren't aware of it. And in fact, I checked the jurisprudence and I cannot find any jurisprudence that allows that, and I'm not convinced that that is the rule in any other jurisdiction, national jurisdiction. I've looked for it. I'm not saying that it don't exist. It may exist in someplace, but I'm not aware of it, and I know certainly in the United States since we're going to be applying the federal rules of evidence it would be a mistrial if a Judge were to say to the jurors, "Pay little value, give little value to answers that come from -- from answers from leading questions." The whole purpose of cross-examination is that. So I'm concerned. I would like to know who else on the Bench shares that, because if there are others then we are even more concerned. And of course this may, and I saw this with all due respect, this also may explain why during the proceedings over the last year the Defence has been rushed. If the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that answers from leading questions are irrelevant or have little value, it does two things. One, it means that you are forcing us to ask on cross-examination non-leading questions, which is not consistent with the Rules, but also you're forcing us to put on a case because that would be the only way for us to at least get evidence before the Tribunal which it would -- it believed would have some value, unless of course we conducted cross-examination by asking open-ended questions, and again that is not the process. That is not the procedure. That is not what is being done in other trials. And so I'm concerned of this, because, you know, we need some answer. I can file a written motion if you wish. But I'm concerned it was may become necessary, for at least the Prlic Defence, to determine whether it should request that certain witnesses be brought back to be fully cross-examined. And secondly, whether a mistrial should be declared and to have the trial start all over again, or perhaps other remedies should be sought such as -- well, a whole new trial from the beginning with new Judges. I mention that. I do this with respect, but I am concerned that if we have been -- after a year labouring under the impression that answers from leading questions should have the value whatever the Judges wishes to give it based on the principle of free evaluation of evidence, which is essentially what has been adopted in this Tribunal, then I think that the rules have been changed without giving notice to the parties and without giving them an opportunity to be heard. That's my first submission. My second submission would be, and it's in regard somewhat to the Okun diaries, because as you note we submitted extensive documentation as to what we intended to go into, and Mr. Scott is correct, we had moved for the entire diary to come in. We still think it should come in. It's fair to both parties. But I use this just as an example. Under Rule 82, which concerns joinder and separate trials, it would appear that because of the time limitations there seems to be a violation of this particular Rule because the accused are not accorded the same rights as if such accused were being tried separately. And I am speaking primarily on behalf of Mr. Prlic. He has indicated in the past himself, and I have done so on his behalf, that we have been denied at times the opportunity to fully cross-examine because time had to be divided among the accused. Mr. Prlic doesn't wish to fight with the other accused to try to grab their time, nor should he have to. Each accused should be tried separately in a sense, and so we would also move for a separate trial, for severance, and it could be done one of two ways. Physically give us a separate trial, or when it comes to the computation of time, the time computed for Mr. Prlic, and I would suggest this be done for the other accused, although I don't wish to -- I don't speak for them, but their -- their lawyers can speak up, that the computation of time should be as if that accused is being tried separately and not as a whole. And I say this because you have accused with different positions, number one. And number two, you have accused who are at different levels. Some are civilians; some are military. They have different -- different strategies. And so if we look at the Rules on the protections of the rights of the accused, I think that you have to read Rule 82 in conjunction with Article 21 of the Statute. So based on -- based on what has been happening, especially with some witnesses, not all, but with some critical witnesses, we feel that Mr. Prlic's right to be tried as if he's being tried separately and afforded all of his rights, not some of his rights, not part of his rights, not rights in conjunction with other accused, for all those reasons we ask that his case be severed from the rest. So I have two oral submissions. One, I wish to know who else among the Bench is of the opinion that answers from leading questions have little value. I also wish to know are we applying all of the rules of the federal rules of evidence? Are we applying some? What are the rules that we are applying so we at least have some guidance. And of course, the second motion is for severance. I do so without filing written motions only because I think it saves time, and I don't wish to prolong the situation, but I think this is of a critical issue that should be dealt with as expeditiously as possible, and if we could file motions it should be done so with the expectation that the parties be given shorter time to respond and to reply. Thank you. And I don't know if my colleagues wish to add to any of this, but I certainly have not consulted them with this, these two submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of General Petkovic is equally highly concerned and shares the concern of Mr. Karnavas and the Prlic Defence with respect to the statement made by Judge Trechsel last week with respect to the relatively --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Listen to my answer first, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- cross-examination. I do apologise but I'd like to add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem with regard to translation, interpretation. I can't hear you, the French interpretation. Could you please resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying that I completely share the Defence of Mr. Prlic with respect to the mention made by Mr. Trechsel last week, the statement made by Judge Trechsel, but with respect to the proposal of measures, I do think we should hear the explanations given by Judge Trechsel, because from the proceedings so far we could conclude that Judge Trechsel was not referring to cross-examination and leading questions and did not mean what one would be able to conclude from what he said last week. Now, with respect to the oral submissions of Mr. Karnavas, I would like to remind you that the Defence of General Petkovic reminded the Trial Chamber several times that all rights should be accorded to the accused on all questions with respect -- on all questions and with respect to the question of time that the Defence has. We always indicated this fact and the fact that we must have as much time as if we were conducting individual trials. So I would like to express my agreement with everything that Mr. Karnavas said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that you were about to give Judge Trechsel the floor beforehand, but if you want to hear from all parties, I'll be brief, just to say that I completely agree with Mr. Karnavas's proposal, and mutatis mutandis we need to understand what he said with respect to his client, Mr. Prlic, and again for my accused, Mr. Praljak. But I'm very interested in hearing the positions that Judge Trechsel has to state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before Judge Trechsel speaks, let's hear Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think the Chamber knows that I try to be economic with my time and I try to keep my comments as brief and concise as possible but sometimes I feel if I don't say something, that somehow will then come back to the disadvantage of the Prosecution either now or at some point in the future. So I do want to address this briefly. First off, Your Honour, in my long years of practice, most of which has been in the common law system up until the last nine years, I have heard comments frankly similar to the one Judge Trechsel made. I've heard that comment made a number of times and in fact I think even in this courtroom I've heard some of the Defence counsel say they'd rather hear a narrative of the witness and hear the witness's own answers as opposed to the words and answers of counsel. So in that context and I think to be fair to Judge Trechsel the comment I made -- perhaps he wanted to be provocative and unusual but I have to say it's not that unusual. I've heard similar statements to that made over the almost 30 years of my practice, and it has always, virtually always better to it hear the narrative and the words of a witness, be it a Prosecution witness or a Defence witness, than the words of counsel in most instances, and I think that statements should be made in that context. Number two, of course this institution draws on a wide body of law. Not that it's controlling, but there is a wealth of law out there that's developed over the past number of -- of thousands of years, different codes, the civil law system, the American system, of course the English system. I see Mr. Stewart's not here, but I also indicate since he also likes to defend the English system. But we draw on wisdom from everywhere, and I don't think again Judge Trechsel's comments were made to say that we are, you know, wholesale incorporating the federal rules of evidence from the US federal system. I don't think we take the rules from any national system. We do look at various systems for wisdom and the things that we can learn from those systems and the points of law that many of them have in common. Many of them have common principles somewhat -- with some variations, and I don't think there's anything unusual about what again Judge Trechsel has said in this regard. Sometimes we may refer to the law of France. Some day we may refer to the law of England and Wales, maybe Swiss law and Hungarian law, searching for the law that best suits the situation in reaching and doing substantive fairness. I'm sure that's the spirit in which the comment was made, and we object to -- we oppose the motion that's been made, and hope it will be taken, those comments, in that context. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have the floor. I must say I have listened with amazement and shaking my head at that long speech Mr. Karnavas gave which I think is a thing completely made up due to a misunderstanding which I find very difficult to understand how the misunderstanding could have come up. I recall the context in which this observation was made, namely in an accused questioning a witness not in the area covered -- covered by main examination, which means that in fact he was conducting a direct examination of the witness. Now, direct examination is not supposed to be given by ways of -- of leading questions, and you, Mr. Karnavas, have sometimes used this even when it was not appropriate. You have intervened I don't know how many times on this. And the reason makes sense, because if you throw a series of sentences which contain the answer to witness and he just says yes or no, you don't know what the witness actually knows himself. He doesn't give any of his information, and in this sense I think leading questions rightfully should be banned from direct examination, be it direct examination of one party or the other, and be it direct examination, as it were, in the void, or direct examination which is for reasons of practicality accepted in the framework of cross-examination. In no way could one in good faith interpret my remark as saying that in cross-examination there is no value in leading questions. I have not said that. I have never meant it. And I must say I'm very amazed that this should be alleged in my face.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, and other Judges, on May 2nd, 2007, in the transcript page 17896, line 21, to 17897, I believe it's line 2, that's where everything all lies. So I'm just looking at what was on the record. I understand the context. I understand Rule 611, and 611, there's a whole body of law we can address that. And also if you look at 611 carefully, you will see that even if you go outside the scope of direct examination, if you were to be questioning on one's credibility, leading questions are permitted under Rule 611. But be that as it may, this is what you stated, sir: "There is no justification for the Defence going into new terrain on a technique that is not allowed on direct but only on cross." Fair enough. Then you go on. "But let me add that at any way answers to leading questions are of little evidentiary value. So the rule in fact goes in favour of the Defence but it's matter of technique." Now, if you look at what you've said, it could be interpreted in one of two ways. Then later on during that -- I do make my record, as is my habit, because I want clarification, and I do ask. I say, "I just -- I just wanted to raise an objection on the record that I don't subscribe to the notion that answers to leading questions are of little evidentiary value. I think this is an incorrect statement of the law, and I think that you have to go on a case-by-case basis, but I am sure that Your Honour didn't actually -- meant literally what --" and I'm cut off at that point. The whole purpose of me raising it at that point in time, and I looked at you, I remember that moment. I looked because I thought perhaps it was a slip of the tongue, perhaps you needed to clarify. But no clarification came. Now, I don't want to be, later on, on appeal, if I have to raise an issue, and they say, Well, wait a second, you haven't got an answer to the question that you posed based on an objection so therefore you either waived it or the interpretation can be given as the one that was provided by Mr. Scott. So that was the whole purpose. And so based -- if we but it into context and what you said, I was -- I was left with the impression, and in fact I commented and I asked a lot of lawyers over the weekend, perhaps 20 or 30 Defence lawyers, do they know if this is -- if this is the rule over here. So if you're telling us now, Judge Trechsel, that the comment that leading questions are of no -- answers to leading questions have little value, if we are talking about areas where direct examination should be conducted, I whole-heartedly subscribe to that. That's the purpose of asking direct examination of your own witnesses to get their testimony. It is their testimony, not the Prosecution's testimony. If you're saying that in asking a compound question where there may be many different answers to the question because it's compound, yes to one part, no to another and what have you, maybe to a third, then I would agree that the trier of fact would have a very difficult time in assessing what is that one answer yes to? Is it yes to the first part, the second part, or the third part. And of course that is -- in that event it is the poor technique of the trial lawyer that is at fault. If on the other hand what you're saying is irrespective of the answer that one gets on cross-examination, in other words, if he gets a yes or a no answer from a leading question, that the Trial Chamber will assess that particular answer in context with the question in applying the free evaluation of evidence as is normally done in this Tribunal because it has adopted for all intents and purposes the continental approach of evaluating the evidence, hence why we bring in all this evidence, then again I have no problem with that, and I would -- I would withdraw whatever observations I had made. If, on the other hand, however, it is the Trial Chamber's position that answers to leading questions are of little evidentiary value, there I think, if that is the answer, then of course I think that my client has been prejudiced and I was unaware that that is the rule and that is not the rule. So that's why I ask for this -- I made this oral submission, and that's why I didn't bother to do a written submission. So we all spend alight of time. And that's why I've asked for clarification early on. So it wasn't meant to be offending anybody, but my job is to be due diligent, sir, due diligent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to be clear on this, did you get the clarification and is it satisfactory or do you have more questions open to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe I have -- I believe now -- I'm -- I feel like I understand. What you're saying is if a compound question is being asked and -- then you really can't trust -- you as the trier of fact can't trust the answer and that's an absolute certainty. I think we can all agree on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In my view we are in full agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And I think we always were, but there was -- perhaps I have expressed myself in a misleading way or have not insisted. I've tried to be brief, too, so maybe I'm a bit too brief sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's why I was -- I was trying to be helpful, Your Honour, last Wednesday, and when I didn't receive a response I thought, well, silence could be acquiescence. That's -- so there was no -- there was no intent to offend. That's not my purpose here, because at the end of the day my client's life rests in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I take that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We've just spent 30 minutes dealing with procedural matters. I've listened to a -- with a great deal of interest to what has been said by Mr. Karnavas and by my fellow Judge. It seems to me, but I did not believe that such a matter would cause such a stir, it seemed to me that during the last hearing -- just before my fellow Judge made some submissions about this matter, it seems to me that I said myself that an accused or a Defence counsel may ask a leading question. I said that before, before, and you can check it by reading the transcript. I stated that this was an allowed practice, and that of course the Judges would assess the answer given to the leading question. So the matter had been resolved already at that point. And I had the feeling that my fellow Judge was making a side comment on a matter that was not related to the direct examination but to something completely different, something related to Rule 90(H)(iii) where it is stated that the Trial Chamber may allow questions related to other matters. And I believe that the question put by Mr. Praljak was a question allowed by Rule 90(H)(iii). And may I add that the Trial Chamber is allowed to refuse such questions that are asked. But the Trial Chamber was extremely fixable and allowed Mr. Praljak to put his question to the witness and the debate was not on whether the question was a leading question or not. That's what we can say about the matter, and we are going to have the witness brought in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Before asking you to take the solemn declaration, please give us your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Grant Finlayson, date of birth, 24th of the 6th, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: New Zealand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have an occupation and, if so, what is that occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My occupation is a marine technical consultant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you already testified before an International Tribunal on the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or is it the first time you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask you to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me give you some information about the way this testimony is going to be organised throughout the week. As you know, you will testify today until Thursday. You are a Prosecution witness. You will first answer questions put to you by the Prosecution. The representatives of the Prosecution are sitting on your right. You've probably met them this morning or during the weekend. Following this stage of the testimony during which the Prosecution will put a number of documents to you, you will then have to answer questions put to you by the Defence counsel, who are on your left. You can see that are many of them. They are here to represent each one of them the interests of one accused. At some point some of the accused also might have some questions to put to you. You've told us that this is the first time you've testified before an international tribunal, so you might be a bit unsettled by some of the questions put to you. You will soon realise that the questions put to you by the Prosecution are questions that are not leading, that are as neutral as possible, and the questions put to you by the Defence counsel or by the accused themselves might be leading in their nature. The four Judges who are sitting before you may, as per the rule, ask any -- at any moment questions to you, but we have recently decided to wait for the parties to have completed their examination before putting questions to the witnesses. Of course we might decide to intervene if we deem it absolutely necessary. Please try when answering the questions put to you to be as concise and as clear as possible, because what's important here is the answers you provide to the questions put to you, and that's why you have before you this screen where you can see the transcript of the words uttered by each and every one of us here. If at some point you do not understand one of the questions put to you, do not hesitate the one putting the question to repeat it. Every one hour and a half we'll have a break for technical purposes, but also to allow you to take a rest, because you will soon realise that to answer questions for hours on end is something that is quite tiring. If at any time you feel unwell, do not hesitate to tell us, and I will then decide to take a break. If at any moment you feel that you need to address the Chamber, you may do so. These are just a few words about the way we are going to proceed. I'm now going to give the floor to the Prosecution, and the Prosecution will now start with the examination-in-chief. Let me remind the representatives of the Office of the Prosecution that they have to ask non-leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Finlayson.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Finlayson could I ask you first some questions on your background. Could you tell the Court what has been your educational background?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: My educational background was I was at a secondary school in New Zealand, obviously, until the year of 1990 -- 1974, and I went to what we term as a fifth form level at high school. I completed my university entrance after I joined the royal New Zealand navy at the age of 16, and that's as far as my education goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you said 1975 you joined the Royal New Zealand Navy. How long did you serve the royal New Zealand navy?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I served in the navy for 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what -- can you briefly tell us what you did in those 20 years?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I joined the -- when I joined the navy I joined as an apprentice -- apprentice control electrical artificer [phoen] they referred it to. That's -- I went up through the ranks up to what is termed chief petty officer, which would be equivalent to a sergeant in the army. I then commissioned. I eventually left the royal New Zealand navy as a lieutenant commander, weapons engineering officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And that -- so -- and that was in 1970 -- in 1995 that you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- that you were commander -- yeah. Is it true that during this period that you served as an UNMO officer in Bosnia-Herzegovina from March 1993 until March 1994?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And before serving did you get any specific training as to this function?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: The training -- I received quite thorough training in New Zealand, and in fact I received two lots of training initially, and I can't remember the exact times at this stage, but I was told that I'd be going to Bosnia, in fact probably -- it must have been around October the year before I eventually went. We did -- I think it was around a week's training. Pretty comprehensive regards how demilitarised zones work and how UNMOs generally go about their duties. We had obviously first aid, weapons recognition, language, and first aid, anything you'd maybe relate with the requirements. At the end of that training it was -- I assumed -- I was told -- in fact I wasn't pulling at that time and it wasn't until six months later that I was eventually posted to UNPROFOR to replace my predecessor from the Royal New Zealand Navy, Commander Reace. At that time, I underwent I think about another three or four days' training, and that was in New Zealand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it correct that around March 1993 you then travelled to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That's -- that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it correct that you would travel to Zagreb and that you had some further training there? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We -- on arrival in Zagreb, we underwent - I think it was again three days - training in the UNMO headquarters in the Zagreb headquarters there. Again, repeating mainly first aid and some driving techniques and a few other essential skills that they thought would be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was waiting for my colleague to go back to that, but it's obviously not been corrected. When the witness was introducing himself, the oral interpretation we received was that the witness's occupation was that of a technical consultant with the marines' corps, brings as a branch, a military branch, and now we've seen all these questions regarding geography, and it appears to be no mere coincidence. That's at least what it seems. So if my learned friend could please ask a question about the witness's present profession so we don't have to go back to that during our cross-examination, because this is so patently wrong. What I talked about was at page 20, line 4. That's what my objection concerns. It was a matter of oral interpretation more so than a matter of the actual transcript, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Finlayson, you've heard what counsel said. You have any comments to made on this?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I think I understood. He misunderstood my occupation. My occupation at this time is not with the marines. It is a marine technical consultant. What I do is, I consult. It's probably -- it needs further explanation perhaps. I consult to the likes of ship owners or insurance companies on matters -- technical matters regarding vessels, ships, and aquacultural farms and structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Finlayson. I think that clarifies the point raised. Now, is it correct that you then travelled to -- to -- that you were stationed in Medjugorje, Bosnia-Herzegovina at the UNMO BiH south office in March 1993?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, can you describe what you saw as the role of the UNMO in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: To be perfectly honest, I don't believe that role was clearly defined at the time. Throughout my training both in New Zealand and even in Zagreb, a clear terms of reference was never given. As most people will be aware, a military observer normally observes peace in a demilitarised zone, or certainly that was my understanding of it. We didn't have peace in Bosnia. We didn't have a demilitarised zone. So the -- so the clarity of our role was really non-existent. We, however, established ourselves, and I think it was throughout the former Yugoslavia, as a source of -- I think the main roles that we had or that were agreed was that we provided eyes for the international community. We provided feedback on what was actually happening within the former Yugoslavia. We in a lot -- we provided a means of communication between the -- between the parties. We gave assistance with the likes of UNHCR for -- for assisting in the facilitating of convoys for -- of aid to the civil population. We -- we also attended to things like prisoner exchanges, body exchanges, and other such like activities. That would be the main -- main roles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to now ask you to look at an exhibit, and you will be provided with a bundle of exhibits that we will go through today and maybe a part of tomorrow, and I would like you to look at Exhibit 00487. Now, Witness, this a document from the chief military observer, and the subject is entitled: "Concept for the deployment of UNMO in the Bosnia-Herzegovina command." Now, I would like to draw your attention first to paragraph 5 where it talks about UNPROFOR -- UNPROFOR's task under this mandate. Let me first ask you, in the area that you operated in the -- in the south Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there an UNPROFOR battalion also stationed?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, there was. The Spanish Battalion was also in Medjugorje and later established a secondary base in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, could I draw your attention to paragraph 6 of this -- of this document, and I'll read it out for you. It says the following: "UNMO teams will be attached under operational control of each battalion. They are best used in a mobile negotiating, reporting and reconnaissance role. They may be based in one location, for example, with the battalion headquarters, or in a number of locations within the battalion area if the situation so dictates." Can I ask you to comment on what's been said here as far as the relationship between UNMO and an UNPROFOR battalion? So I assume in this case SpaBat. How would you comment on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Firstly we weren't -- we weren't under the operational control of the battalions when we first joined -- or when I first joined the UNMO organisation. Having said that, we were very closely in communication. We weren't sited within the battalion although that changed during my time in Bosnia. We were all UNMO headquarters, sector headquarters were collocated with the battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if you say that you -- that you weren't on the operation -- that you were not on the -- under the operational control of the battalion, does that mean that the UNMO acted completely independently?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I think to say it operated completely independently would be incorrect. However, it had its own command structure. However, the communication between the battalion and the UNMOs was such that there was -- cooperation would be probably a better word to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Could I ask you now to direct your attention to paragraph 9 of this document, which is on the next page of this document. And I'll read it out again. It says: "Nature of task. The UNMOs will perform the following nature of tasks: "Patrolling in the area of responsibility. "Liaison with concerned parties. "Negotiation with authorities as required. "Inevitable/ad hoc humanitarian tasks." Would this encompass what you've just told us as well?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I believe that aligns with what I previously listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's now talk about the organisational structure of the UNMO. Is it correct, Mr. Finlayson, that over the weekend I asked you to draw up a diagram of the organisational structure of the -- of the United Nations military observers?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to happened over the following piece of document to the witness, and if we can put this on the overhead projector, please. And maybe we could first get an IC number for this document. Can I ask the registry to assign an IC number to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will become IC 536.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, please write your name on this document and today's date, please. This is to authenticate the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Finlayson, I will adjust asking maybe if you can explain what you've written down here.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Well, essentially I just said that -- that the UNMOs had had their own command structure. This was essentially it as I recall it. I was a bit sketchy on dates when I -- when I put this together, but on around the time of -- of June 1993, the structure was, there was an UNMO headquarters in -- in Zagreb, and that was the overall command, and they were in -- they were in the UNPROFOR headquarters and reported -- they reported to the UNPROFOR HQ. Under that was a secondary headquarters for Bosnia, and that was located in Kiseljak. And directly below UNMO BH command were the individual sectors, and as I recall there was a sector -- a separate sector in Sarajevo. What have I got here? Sector north. UNMO BH South, which is our own sector. UNMO central, and another one in Bihac, in the Bihac pocket. There were, I believe, UNMOs in -- well, there were UNMOs in Pale, Zepa, and Gorazde. In BH South we had five teams. They're shown here with their call-signs above them. Mike X-ray 1 is in Nevesinje. Mike X-ray 3 was in Bileca. MX4 was in Jablanica. Mike X-ray 5 was in East Mostar. And I think later on Mike X-ray 6 came along in West Mostar. We think that was around September. During -- later on during my time as -- as SMO, which was after September, we set up teams in Tomislavgrad, Posusje, and Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of questions clarification of this diagram. First of all, I notice that there -- that you haven't marked MX2. What is the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: MX2, as I understand it there were three teams on the Serbian side of the confrontation line. However, that was before I -- I joined the team, and that was disbanded. I think that was in Labunja [phoen], but I may have the name incorrect there so, I think ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is it correct that MX1, MX2, and MX3 were all on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And let me just ask another -- questions about who was the top man in your -- in UNMO, the chief military observer?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: The chief military observer for most of the time I was there was Bo Pellnas, General Bo Pellnas from Sweden.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So he was stationed in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: He was stationed in Zagreb, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And where would you have fitted in, in this diagram, first upon your arrival in June -- or in May 1990 -- no, March 1993?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: In -- sorry. When I arrived, I worked from what is shown there as MX, which was an UNMO headquarters, which was located in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And -- and what was your function in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Sorry, you've gone to June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yeah, which is the date, I think --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- of this diagram.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: During June 1993 I was a team leader, and in fact I set up the Mike X-ray 5 team in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And just one more question. Upon your arrival, who was the person in charge of UNMO BH South?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: At the time of my arrival it was a Major Paul Ronksley from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was his title?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Sorry. He was the senior military observer, BH South.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it correct that later on in September 1993 when you returned to Mostar that you -- which function did you then form in this diagram?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I took over from -- in fact, sorry, I didn't take over from Paul Ronksley. There had been one in between. But I took over as the senior military observer, BH South.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you now something to say about the way the reporting system functioned within the UNMO? And, well, maybe, if you still need the diagram --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: No, I think we can get away without it. Okay. The -- if you recall, the lowest level of that -- of that diagram were the teams out in the various locations around the sector. Effectively they reported in to the headquarters for the sector, i.e., all the MX1, 3, 4, 5, 6 reported in at the end of each day to Mike X-ray, which was the sector headquarters. They did that essentially by HF or UHF coms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you explain what that is, H --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Well, high frequency or ultra high frequency coms. Just a radio, a click-click radio. Very unreliable, very -- sorry, not -- yeah, unreliable and tricky at times. Often the link wasn't perfect, so we relied on information being relayed by other -- other parties at times. That information would be compiled at the headquarters. That -- the BH South headquarters would then put together a report at the end of each day of their activities and any activity that had taken place. In the case of BH South, that was forwarded to the UNMO BH command. That was generally done via the SpaBat or the Spanish Battalion's communications centre. It then went to BH command. BH command then coordinated all the reports from the other sectors into a BH command report which then went to UNMO Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you say that it was communicated at the -- at the Spanish Battalion communications centre, how was it communicated?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Again, that was via -- their communications centre, I would guess it was probably -- I am assuming it would be by HF, high frequency equipment which they would have had which would not have been as vulnerable to the terrain, interruptions from the terrain, and they would have had the equipment to receive that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now let's move back to March 1993, when you arrived in Medjugorje. Could you tell us, what was the situation like at the time in the area, and what did you do in the first two months?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: March -- when I first arrived there the -- essentially the BiH and the HVO were combined in their efforts against the Serbs, Bosnian Serbs. The activity at that time was fairly low key. It was obvious that -- that there had been heavy fighting obviously over the previous year, but at that time it was -- it was fairly quiet. It became apparent that there was disharmony between the -- the two parts of -- of the force, i.e., the -- the HVO and the BiH. So -- but that was tense at those periods and the activity was -- was low.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've said that -- it was apparent that there was disharmony between the HVO and the BiH. What had caused this disharmony, as you -- as you've put it?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I think -- I don't think I'm really in a position to say what -- what caused it, but I became aware of it through discussions with -- with -- with the various lower key headquarters. I think I made an observation, and possibly it wasn't well-founded, but I think at the time it there was the Vance-Owen Plan kicking around, and that seemed to -- seemed to be maybe fuelling a bit of the distrust and -- between the various parties, and I think that eventually led from memory to the HVO in our area, asking the BiH -- their BiH partners to lay down their weapons or give up their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you some clarification on what you just said. You said that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan fuelled distrust. Can you explain a bit better to the Judges what you meant -- what you mean by that? Why did it fuel distrust between the HVO and the BiH?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I will -- I will do so, but I also just caution that at that point in time I was fairly new in the -- in the area and new to the situation, and I would say that I also hadn't come totally to terms with it at that point in time, but the -- the Vance-Owen Plan, as I recall, allocated certain areas. The governance, as I saw it, of certain areas to either Muslim parties or -- or Croatian, or Bosnia Croatian parties, and that I guess within the Balkans there was a history there, and there was essentially a mistrust. So that's -- I think that's where my comments came -- came from on that -- that particular point. In other words, the -- the people were not -- if you were in the wrong -- the wrong area, you weren't really too keen on the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In your uptake, was the Vance-Owen Peace Plan publicly known in the area?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: It appeared to be known, and I think there were -- from memory, I believe there were a couple of versions of it, and as it grew. That's my memory, and it may be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did there come a time in April that -- that the chief military observer visited your area?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it was April. I'd have to refer to my diary for exact points, but at -- at a point in -- yes, it would have been late April. Mid to late April the chief military observer was Bo Pellnas, and he came to BH South. I being a new UNMO -- and for your information, UNMOs, regardless of their rank, all go in as an UNMO. The rank goes out the door. But as an UNMO, I had the prestigious job of driving that day, so I was told to go and collect the -- the general from the airport. So that was my role.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know why -- why did he come to the area?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: At the time when I went to get him I knew nothing, and really my knowledge of what was happening grew during the day. The -- we effectively left Split where we airlifted him and proceeded directly, I think, directly to the Mostar hospital on the west side where he had a meeting with the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit 2054, please. Can you explain to the Court what document -- what kind of document this is?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: This is reporting on the CM activities in Mostar in 1993, 18th of -- 18th to 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if -- if we read the document it starts off with 18 April 1993, and I'll just read out the first part of this paragraph. "At 2.30 a meeting was held in Mostar together with ECMM and the representatives for the Muslim and Croat communities. From the Muslim side, Vice-President Ganic was the head of mission --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Bos reads too much of this out, may we please established whether the witness attended the meeting and has any knowledge of what happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, did you attend the meeting that Bo Pellnas was --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I did not attend the meeting. I was in attendance directly outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So what did you do at the time that Mr. Pellnas was at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: At that stage I -- I simply remained in the vehicle and -- which was immediately outside the venue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, this document refers to a couple of people who attended this meeting. Did you see those persons yourself? Let me first ask. Mr. Ganic. Did you see Mr. Ganic?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I believe I entered in my diary that Mr. Ganic was there, but I -- I personally can't recall him at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What about General Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, I recall being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And Mr. -- Vice-president Prlic. Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I've got a slight recollection, but -- yes, slight.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And -- and what about General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: General Petkovic definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was this the first time that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, we could save a lot of time. Just because he can identify certain persons that were at the meeting does not qualify the gentleman to comment about the contents of the meeting or the contents of the meeting as described in this particular document, and I think it would be a waste of time to simply try to get the gentleman to simply acknowledge what happened at the meeting when he himself wasn't there, and in all fairness to the gentleman, it's putting him on the spot and having him try to recollect what he might have remembered others told him of a meeting that he didn't attend but, rather, was sitting in his car, you know, chilling out, as it were. I think it's guess to just move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not going to ask him, you know, what happened in the meeting and then what he knows what was discussed in the meeting, and we will have another witness to do that, but I do think I can ask some questions, and my questions on this document will be limited to what he can actually testify to. And I'm not going to go through this whole document page by page, but there are a couple of things which I think I can ask him as far as his presence at the meeting of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he can ask the questions of the gentlemen without the document. That's my whole point. And if they're going to bring in another witness to question that witness about the document or meetings in a document I think we can hear that testimony then. Let's just get the testimony of what this gentleman knows and observed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we've reached the following situation: There is a meeting, and the witness is sitting in a vehicle outside. After the meeting, will General Pellnas tell him what happened at the meeting? If we -- he has seen a number of people; has he seen Mr. Prlic? Let's try and again some time, because Defence counsel will object, and we shall lose precious time, in particular if another witness is going to come and testify about these matters. Unless there is something else you would like to say or unless this is a really usually issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll -- I understood what you said, and I'll move on very quickly through this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you -- that you saw Mr. Petkovic there.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Mr. Petkovic was there, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was this the first time that you saw Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I seem to feel that the Prosecutor's insisting -- by-passing your instructions and all these matters and the Prosecutor said, Well, we have a list of witnesses and a certain amount of time when somebody who attended the meeting and who compiled this report will come into the courtroom as a witness, and I think the Prosecutor has envisaged that for June or July. So do we really need to insist upon these matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't hear anything. The interpreters could not be heard. It's working now. I'm turning to the Prosecution. You asked the witness, "Have you seen Mr. Petkovic?" I think before that you should ask him whether he knew Mr. Petkovic, because you could have told him, "Did you see Mr. Scott?" I don't know. Mr. Petkovic is just there?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did ask him whether he saw Mr. Petkovic there and he did agree that he saw Mr. Petkovic there. So my next question was, was that the first time you saw Mr. Petkovic? And he just affirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And so, Mr. Finlayson, again just to follow up on that, did you have any dealings with Mr. Petkovic later on? Maybe, you know, not directly at that day but later on in your duties as an UNMO officer.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I did on several occasion. During that day we were introduced, or certainly Mr. Petkovic and all the players at the time were identified to us. Essentially it was -- the other person with me was the SMO, who was Paul Ronksley, and he was making the effort to explain what was happening and who was attending.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Pellnas after -- after the meeting, told you about what the meeting was about and what resulted at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting ended up -- I mean, we witnessed I think it was Mr. Stojic storming out, and then of course the meeting had ended up in disarray, and from memory -- so the -- it was quickly accounted to us that, and I think Mr. Petkovic had at that particular meeting had refused to talk to Mr. Pasalic because he was of the wrong rank --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Sorry,, I'm really -- I'm sorry to interrupt. I really don't see what probative value this has at all. They've got other witnesses, apparently, who were present during this meeting. I think we've all -- in fact had already testify -- one witness who was present during the meeting on another occasion. And I object to this. This is of no probative value that one can measure whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness says, I witnessed -- I think it was Mr. Stojic [Realtime transcript read in error "Petkovic"] storming out. He himself says he witnessed it, so this is clearly probative -- probative evidence. I -- I really don't understand the objection. He says he witnessed it himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask him to clarify in that case. He's in the car. Perhaps he's listening to the radio or reading a newspaper. Did he know Mr. Stojic? I don't know anything. This is my position. I hold a meeting. There's somebody in a car, and there's somebody storming out of the meeting. Seemingly this was Mr. Stojic. Did he know him before that? Did he get to know him after that? What is the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I was about to clarify that when I was interrupted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I'd like to correct an error in the transcript. Page 39, line 9, the question by Mr. Scott did not refer do my client, Petkovic, as has been recorded, but it is the second accused. So could that name be put right, please. Not Mr. Scott; Mr. Bos. I apologise to both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at any rate the time has come for a break. It's a quarter to 4.00. Let's have a 20-minute break. We shall resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Bos, just a minor observation. Regarding the document you want to submit to the witness, 2054, it has been admitted already through another witness. If you want to put questions on this document, well, this witness has to bring some added value with regard to the document, otherwise we're wasting time. The document has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, some of the conclusions of this document has a direct effect on the work of this witness in the days that followed the meeting we've discussed just before the break, and that's why this document is important for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Finlayson, that's -- was going to be my next question. Is the meeting that Mr. Pellnas participated there on the 18th of April resulted in some specific tasks in which you got involved in the days that followed, and what were those tasks?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: This -- this meeting -- on conclusion of this meeting it was agreed that a joint commission meeting was established in Mostar, and in fact I think it -- if I recall, it happened that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And were you involved in setting up this joint commission meeting?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That particular -- the first meeting I -- I still was -- I attended the meeting, but I was not involved in setting that up. Once at a later stage the joint commission was set up, and I think that was maybe a day or even two later. Without referring to my diaries, I'm not too sure. I was tasked to actually take control of the joint operations centre for the UNMOs by General Pellnas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what -- can you give a bit more detail what -- what you mean by, "take control of the joint operations centre"? What did that entail?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yeah. I guess "take control" is really -- was to chair the meetings and at that stage the idea of the joint operations centre at that point was to monitor what was happening in the region. Effectively the -- because of the -- the break-up of the teams, there were -- there were rumours arife around what was happening, from one region to one group of people and the other. One side would have -- have obvious concerns of their people in one area, while the opposite side would -- had problems with their people in another area. So the idea of the operations centre was to send out, investigate these reports with members of UNPROFOR and members of both the BiH and the HVO and that each party investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you participate in any of these joint patrols that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Affirmative. I did. One of them was -- can I -- can I refer to my diary, or is it -- I'm just -- some of the names escape me, but I had one up north to a Muslim-controlled area where there were fears of a group of Bosnian Croatian civilians living in that area. So that was one patrol we did. And the other patrol was to a -- or to attempt to get to the area of Sovici, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just first. You've been referring to a diary. Let's clarify this issue first. Is it correct -- what are you referring to when you say, "Can I refer to my diary"? What diary are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes. You have my diary I've given to you for your use. If I were to give accurate information it would just be handy to refer to it to make sure I've got the names of the cities correct or the town correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this diary was disclosed on the 25th of April, also to the Defence, and I -- the witness -- the Prosecution doesn't intend to introduce this diary as an exhibit in these proceedings, but if the witness wants to refer to the diary, I -- I think he can in order to -- to jog his memory on certain names and places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may -- if I may, Your Honour. I would suggest that first a foundation be laid, something a little bit more than just asking one question. And assuming that the diary's only being looked at, once a foundation has been made and I invite the gentleman to lay in a proper foundation how it was kept why it was kept there are direct quotes are they the essence of what was said so we don't have what -- so we don't have problems as we did with one particular witness. Once a foundation is laid, then if it is for the purpose of refreshing the gentleman's memory he can refer to the diary whenever he needs to provided it's noted on the record he's referring to the diary to refresh the memory. That would be my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One minute, Mr. Kovacic. I would like to tell the Defence counsel that they should not sort of exaggerate or fall in the trap of procedural matters, which makes it so that everybody wastes time. In 1993, so over 14 years ago, the witness took part in matters. Fourteen years he's come here to testify to documents. Of course he can't remember anything or he may remember specific things, some of them. So, Witness, you met the OTP before you came. When did you arrive in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Saturday morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how many hours did you spend together with the OTP before your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would guess probably around 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So during these 10 or so hours, did you look at the diary which you mention every time, every minute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- I think just where I -- I stumbled a little bit there was the names of the cities, and even as we -- or the towns, and even as we're talking they've come to my mind, and I guess if you're happy with that, I'm happy to proceed without the diary. But every so often it's -- I guess it's like a security blanket. It's nice to look down and check to see you're saying the right thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say this as I think I have in the case of other witnesses, that giving evidence should be not a test of -- always of memory so much as accuracy, and if the witness is assisted by looking at his diary, I certainly would have no objection to that. In the interest of transparency, let me say when it comes to cross-examination, he's going to be reading quite a bit of during my questioning, so I have no objection to him looking at it now if it would assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is true that the OTP disclosed the diary to the Defence in late April, the 25th or the 26th, I believe. We did have a chance to look at it. Unfortunately, however, we didn't have a chance to familiarise our client with the diary since we did not obtain a translation of the diary, and we simply didn't have the time to get it translated ourselves. Therefore, we were considerably at a disadvantage in terms of retrieving further documents from our clients. So this diary, especially if anyone is intending to tender it, must be qualified by saying this: The clients were not served this document in a language they can understand, although I certainly think that this diary belongs to the group of documents that must be translated and served to the accused in -- in a language that they can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, as usual, has had an excellent suggestion. He believes that the diary could be useful to the witness for him to refresh his memory as to dates and names, not as to the substance that is going to be cross-examined. But we're going to deliberate on this to see whether we authorise the use of the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After deliberations, the Trial Chamber sees no position, no -- to the diary being used to guide the witness for him to provide details, but the Trial Chamber requests from the Prosecution that they ask the witness how he wrote this diary, why he did so, why was he keeping a diary, what did he mention in it, in order to lay the foundation of the existence of this diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Finlayson, I think you've heard what the -- what the Presiding Judge just said. Can you tell it us a little built more how you kept this diary?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I'm actually starting to believe I should carry on without it, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I kept a -- I kept a diary. It was a personal diary. It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But when did -- you noted down these -- your notes in this diary? Was this --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: You can hardly call it a diary. It just had some notes of key points that occurred to me only, and it was -- basically at the end of most days I just jotted down what I had done on those days. It contains some personal opinions, but as I say, I was going to use it to get some names, and they have come to mind. So maybe we should proceed without it and see how I go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you have the diary here with you?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: No. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you have it in the witness room?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I thought you had it as a piece of paper. So I'm happy to proceed without it, I think. Let's get this show on the road, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Get going.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right, we'll continue. But, Mr. Finlayson, if there comes a time when your diary will become helpful, just please indicate this and we'll -- we'll provide you with a copy of your diary maybe after the break. Now, you -- you said that you couldn't find a name of a certain village and that it now -- that it came back to your memory. What was the name of that village?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yeah. It was Ostrozac, which was the first one where the Croatian families were believed to be under threat by the surrounding Muslim-controlled -- controlling people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And were there any other joint patrols in which you participated --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, the one to Sovici and Doljani, Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you give us a bit more information about this particular joint patrol, Sovici or Doljani?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Doljani, yeah. Yeah, that was a patrol where we had to move our way through the Muslim lines. That involved, in fact, moving quite substantial fortifications in the way of concrete blocks. This was done by utilising the Spanish Battalion's APC. We moved -- we moved through -- it took us probably an hour or two to get through, and then we made our way to Doljani, and we then came to the opposition's front line, the HVO's front line where in fact we got stopped and we were unable to proceed much further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What kind of -- of allegations were made as to what had happened in Sovici, Doljani?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Again there was allegation -- sorry, there was belief that Muslim people were being persecuted by -- or mistreated by -- by the controlling Croatian forces in that area.
