So it was, to follow up, the day before we looked for -- for beliefs that Croatians were getting harmed. This was to follow up the belief that Muslims were being harmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said you were stopped at the -- at the opposition front line, at the HVO's front line. Who stopped you there?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: A group of soldiers. They -- I can't recall what they were wearing, to be honest. None of them spoke the local language. My Croatian interpreter was of no use. Luckily I had a Danish UNMO with me who could speak German, which appeared to be the only language this group of soldiers knew. And they were reasonably hostile in their attitude towards us. They eventually let us return but certainly would not let us proceed to Doljani.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, this was a joint patrol, so I assume there was an HVO representative in this patrol as well. Did the HVO representative undertook any action to -- to let your patrol pass through this -- through this check-point?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I can't recall who it was, but it was general practice that they did get out and talk. Whether it was HVO or armija, we regularly had problems with it being ineffective. They weren't recognised, or there was a game being played out. We never really knew. But the thing was that they more often than not were -- didn't prove to be a great asset.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What did you conclude as to who these soldiers were who were speaking German and not the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I think I can -- well, I did. I concluded they were probably a group of mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And for which army would they have been serving?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: They were -- they would have been serving for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to move on now to about the 9th of May, but just before I do, can I ask you whether you remember any particular incident on a joint patrol that involved Colonel Pasalic just prior to the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes. It was a -- it was a joint patrol I wasn't on, but I remember -- I recall that his -- the -- I can't remember the exact details, but I believe -- no. I know his progress was stopped, and his return to Mostar was -- was presented it the an HVO check-point up the Neretva River on the northern side of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And on what day was this?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: The 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What happened on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: On the 9th of May a -- a concerted attack on the Muslim parts of the town of Mostar was -- was launched by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How did you learn about this attack?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't recall how I learnt about it, but certainly we -- we got to know about it from some of our earlier patrols, I would guess, but I can't recall how we learnt about that attack unfolding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what did you do on that day when you learned about this?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: On that day we were tasked by the SMO at the time, Paul Ronksley, to head into Mostar to -- to find out what was going on. In doing so, our progress, we -- we were stopped going into Mostar from the south end through where we normally entered. So we then tried to enter, I guess, from the western end, western side, and again we were prevented from going in. And then eventually I myself found a small road which led us around to the north end of the town, and we were able to establish a position to -- to view what was happening. And also another team also managed to get a little bit further in the south and establish an OP to the south of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And at the position where you eventually got, did you notice anything in the neighbourhood of that position?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: There was a tank immediately adjacent to us. Effectively I would guess that -- that there was two or three tanks, and from memory I think at least one artillery piece, but I can't honestly sit here and recall that accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said there was a tank immediately adjacent. To which army did that tank belong?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That was HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, behind you I've set up a -- a map of Mostar and the surrounding area, and could I ask you to mark the location where you eventually got on the 9th of May and where you observed the situation on the 9th in the town.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you mark that dot, please, with a number A -- A.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you said that you also observed a tank very close to you. Where -- could you mark the location of the tank, please?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could it mark it with a number B.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you've said that you also noted a few more tank. Can you mark the locations of the other tanks that you observed that day?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You will have to talk into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I think the exact location of that C would be questionable at this time, but I'd put a rating of about 70 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And were -- these two tanks that you've just been marked now were they on elevated positions, because the map doesn't really show, but would that be a hill on which they are?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: It's -- it's certainly a hill that surrounds. The city's in a small valley, really. So there's hill from the back, and there's hills from the Hum all around. So all the positions were pretty well elevated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you see these tanks shooting that day?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And in what direction were they shooting?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Probably -- I'll use this. The tanks were essentially firing in this -- this area here over into the side of the -- again, it's probably -- the accuracy of where we were, they were landing basically around that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you will have to describe for the record the area you just indicated. Could you --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: The area there is essentially the town immediately on the -- on the western side of the Neretva River. It's the commercial centre of Mostar, I think would -- it certainly gave the impression. It had large shops and what looked like houses and banks, et cetera. They were certainly hard to recognise after a year of war, but it certainly looked to be the commercial area, and it was the area where, fair to say, the Muslims -- the Muslim forces had congregated or were still in possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What else did you observe that day?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: At this stage I really -- that was all I -- all I personally observed was -- was the level of activity and giving the information about what was happening in that -- in that area. The -- the OP at the south end of town, they reported that they'd seen civilian being taken out of the town. I, from memory, and I think I put in my statement I didn't see anything, but I think we actually saw the buses but, of course, just going up the hill, we got a glimpse of them, but from where we were they could have been anything, whereas the team down the south could clearly see they were civilians, and they could see that they were civilians being mustered in the -- in the stadium, and the buses were going from the stadium down this road here, I think, if I remember. So the other team was positioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe could you please mark the position of the other team with a number D, please. Mark it as a D.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just to go back to what -- to what you saw that day. You've said that you saw the tanks and that they were shooting. Was there any other weapon that -- was there any other shooting from other weapon --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I think there was. There were definitely mortars being used. I can't remember what was being used up here, but I seem to remember there was a gun up there. It think it may have been an anti-aircraft type weapon, or something like that. Again the memory's gone. I'm sure there was artillery being used at that point, too, and possibly a rocket-propelled grenade, but that may have been later in the piece. I have to be careful there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And was artillery being used by both armies by both the HVO and the ABiH that day?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: The heavy artillery, the armija had none. I think at that stage they probably had -- I think we thought they -- well, we came to the conclusion at that point in time they had seven mortars. Whereas -- so they had no other weapons other than small arms and mortars at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How long did you stay for on that observation point on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I think we -- we stayed until it -- it became dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could get an IC number for this map that was marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you also put the date, today's date, and sign the map. Give us a number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will become IC 537.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, what did you do the next day, on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I believe we tried to get back in to the positions that we'd held the day -- the previous day but were unable to do -- to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And why were you unable to do so?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: We were prevented by the HVO going through any -- through the roadblocks they'd set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So on the 10th of May there was no way of -- of getting into Mostar?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: There was no way of getting into Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what did you do on the 11th of May? Do you recall what you did, what you did that day?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: The exact day I would be unsure of, but I would think that it would be the 11th that we investigated further the -- the fate of the civilians. And we located them, and I can't recall who or how we located them, but we -- we found out they were being held in the -- what we referred to as the Helo factory down in the southern end of down there. And we went down there and worked -- worked to gaining access to find out what was -- what was happening to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you able to enter the Helo factory?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: We were, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Straight away?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Not straight away, but nothing ever happened straight away in Bosnia. I think from memory I noted that it wasn't relatively difficult to actually gain access into that establishment, and once we got there we were shown most -- most -- most things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what -- what you saw --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- that day?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Effectively there were a large number of civilians, and I -- again I can't recall the figure, but I seem to remember it was around the 1.300 mark all up of what I would term civilians. They were mainly predominantly women and children. They were being held in a -- there were two of them being held, and from memory it was a sort of a dormitory, or couple of dormitories, and there were two lots being held in gymnasiums. The ones in the gymnasium were -- in one gymnasium it was -- it was mainly -- it was only men, predominantly older men. There were some what you would term fighting men in that area. The -- the other gymnasium, I think from memory, was a group of people that we believed came from villages -- outlying villages, and I think predominantly from the north. And the women and children that we interviewed had come from Mostar itself. They were all Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit 2293 in your bundle. Look at the second page. This is a report from UNMO BiH south to UNMO headquarters Zagreb. Do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I do. I believe I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, is this a report of -- of what you saw that day at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: It was. It's a report, and it's nothing that I -- aren't happy with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if I could just direct your attention to paragraph 2. It reads: "The people spoken to had stated that they had been taken there against their will. However, had been reassured by the HVO that it was for their own safety." With whom did you actually speak that day?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: We spoke with the women themselves. We tried to -- we were always accompanied by HVO, which made the women very, very nervous. However, we were able to establish a little bit of distance between us, and there were a couple of younger women there that could speak very good English, and they had informed us that they had been dragged out of their homes. I can't recall exactly which night, but one of the preceding nights. And they were there -- they were there against their will. They had nothing. They were not able to take anything with them. They only had the clothes they stood up in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to the next page under paragraph 5. It talks about in total there was, "1.346 people, number supplied by Pusic, another 300 expected tonight. All are Muslims." Is that the figure you've been referring to as --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yeah, and I guess that's where I remembered that figure from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, just to clarify on the name of Pusic, if we go back to paragraph 1 there's a reference here to a person, the commander, Mile Pusic. Is that the person who also provided you the numbers or is this a different Pusic?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I believe it would have been Milo Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If we move to paragraph 6, first sentence, it's -- and I'll read it out: "The initial movement of people was ordered by Mr. Lasic. The people had been taken against their will. Families had been deliberately separated and people not allowed to gather their basic belongings before their transportation." Now, who told you that it was Mr. Lasic?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I would assume that it was Mr. Pusic, but I can't recall. It would have been told by someone if I reported it, someone of authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President. I think it would be a good thing to clarify paragraph 6. This is one person, Mile Pusic, and not a different man Pusic as the Prosecutor mentioned a while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bos. Please have the witness testify who is that person named Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I asked that question, Your Honours, and the witness responded that he believes it's Mile Pusic. That's all he can do. I think I did clarify the whole issue, so I don't really see why -- why I need to do it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, who was this Mile Pusic, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the only time I actually came across Milo [sic] Pusic. I believe he was like a commandant of the establishment. But to be perfectly honest, I think the memory cells have gone on that one, too, Your Honour, but that was my memory of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you pay any other visits to Heliodrom -- to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went following the following day, I think. That was only one more. And then I think I was -- I was required for duty back at the headquarters there for a while, and at a later stage I accompanied General Morillon to -- to the camp, and that was a few days later when there had' been significant international media interest in what was happening in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall any specifics of the visit to Heliodrom with General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: The visit was -- when -- when we arrived in the camp that day, all the women and children had gone. The explanation was they had been relocated. And probably about a significant number of the men had also disappeared with no real explanation other than they'd been relocated to the -- it was indicated they'd been relocated back to their homes. However, a consequent investigation proved that incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You just said consequent investigation proved that incorrect. Could you clarify that sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Well, simply we were able to follow up with a couple of people and find they were at home with a couple of UNMO teams and found out they weren't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you eventually find out where these people went?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Over the -- over the following months really. These people would crop up both in East Mostar. A lot of them ended up in East Mostar. And I -- from memory we -- a few showed up in Jablanica as well. And that was, you know, just as people, various UNHCR people or UNMOs came across them, and at some stage they'd said they'd been in the Helo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That's -- now, earlier we've been discussing the work of -- of these joint commissions and these joint patrols that were being conducted. Now, what -- what happened with the work of the joint commission after the 9th of May? Did -- did that continue, the work of the joint commission?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I believe it did. It -- it continued for -- for some time. However, it -- its effectiveness was reasonably limited, and I think it eventually broke down. I -- yeah. I cannot recall that, but it went for some time, and it was still going when Morillon was there, because we had an -- a joint commission meeting at that -- before we went into the camp. So it went for a little bit longer, but it eventually broke down, but I can't put a days to when it did and I can't really call the specific incident -- incident that made it break down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall that the water supply to East Mostar ever became a topic of discussion in the joint commission?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: The water supply was -- was certainly an issue. East Mostar had no water, and there was -- it was believed that there was the capability to reinstate that from the west side via either a temporary or a permanent line under the Tito -- what was known as the Tito Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And was that line ever established?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: To my memory, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit 2657, please. Now, this is an UNMO report dated the 6th of June, 1993, and I would like to draw your attention to paragraph number F of this report, and I'll read it out. "Utilities: BiH are repeatedly asking for UN assistance with utility restoral, particularly with regard to providing an escort so necessary work can be done on pipeline on Tito bridge. So far, SpaBat has declined to provide escort, as HVO refuse to agree to work stating situation is too dangerous until separation and withdrawal of forces in Mostar complete." Now, I'll continue a little further. It says: "Request that HVO be put on pressure at the highest possible level to allow repair work to proceed ASAP." Does this report summarise the situation as to the water supply?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Certainly my recollection of it would tend to indicate that that was fairly accurate, both the fact that -- that probably the UNPROFOR didn't provide the support and must also the point that the HVO were unwilling to reinstate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time in June that UNMO opened an office in east -- opened an office in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it was about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The 6th of June?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Close to, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now -- and I think you've testified earlier that is it correct that you became the team leader of this -- of this UNMO office in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, and I'll provide you with a map for that, but can you explain to us where the office of UNMO was being established in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yeah. After some --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And maybe we can mark it on two different maps. We can -- you can mark it on this map and also this smaller map of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I -- again, maybe could I ask you to put your initials on this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if we could get an IC number for this map, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And please write today's date, 7th of May. Mr. Registrar, can we have an IC number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. This map will become Exhibit IC 538.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Finlayson, did you also put the date, today's date? Yes. Okay. I'm sorry, it's not visible from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, is there a problem? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, there is, because there are no houses there. These aren't houses. That is hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, can you -- can you explain a little bit more about, you know, this office? How did it look like, where it was situated, and ...

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: You've got me worried now. It was -- it was above the main road that ran from Split to Sarajevo. It was essentially up the hill where I believe I've marked it. There are no roads there, but there are like extended driveways up to a number of houses. So it was quite elevated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that you provided the Prosecution yesterday with a couple of photographs of, you know, of -- depicting this house and also the view that you had from this house?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown, and I think these photographs are in e-court so we can -- we can show them on the e-court, exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll first give a number to the map that we have on screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think that was IC 538. I think it was given an IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So could we look at Exhibit 10000, please, 10000.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It will appear on your screen, Mr. Finlayson, if you just a minute. In fact, the photograph is also in your bundle. We've -- if you look at Exhibit 10000, you will find the photograph there as well.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: It's up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, what is depicted -- depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That's -- that's the -- what became the UNMO office headquarters in East Mostar. It's -- that particular side would be looking out to the west across the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That would have been taken in June at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, we -- we see a flag up there. What kind of flag is that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That's a blue United Nations flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could we move to the next photograph, which is 10001. Okay, Witness, it has appeared now. Could you just again describe to us what's depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That's a -- that's the view from one of the windows in the -- in the UNMO accommodation there, and it's a little built deceiving because it is taken with a telephoto lens. It -- it points down to I think the -- in the Prosecution -- I mean, the Defence may be able to correct me, but I believe the building on the left hand in the foreground was the P -- PPT [sic] building, and that runs -- and the intersection you can see behind it would be the Spanski Square. Behind the right-hand side of the fore-building would be the Tito Bridge area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe since we have it on the screen, Mr. Finlayson, we can actually make markings on this photograph on the screen with an electronic pen. So you've been referring to a couple of places. When you were referring to the PTT building, could you mark that building with the number A, please.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Then you were referring to the -- the Spanish Square?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Spans can I square.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you mark that with a B, please?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you've also bee referring to Tito Bridge. Where would the Tito Bridge have been? Could you mark that with a C.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: [Marks]. It's in behind there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could we get a number for photograph, this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 539.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one question which should have put to you. You said that this picture was taken with a photo [as interpreted] lens through a window of the office. As the crow flies, what is distance between the building and the where this photo was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, between the building at the foreground there? I would say probably less than a kilometre. Less than a kilometre would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what would have been the distance between the UNMO office and point B, the Spanish Square?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Probably around 1.500 metre I would be guessing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And between the Tito Bridge?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: C is probably around 1.100, 1.200.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now move to Exhibit 10002, the next photograph. By the way, this photograph was also taken in June 1993.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What's depict the on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That's -- that's essentially another photograph taken from the same area. That's taken after either I can't recall or an artillery or tank round hit the PTT building there. In the background, again you've got the Spanski Square on the right-hand side, and in the middle of the building in the background I think we always referred to it as a car park. To be honest I'm not a hundred per cent sure whether it was a car park or it just looked like one at the time. And I can't recall what the other buildings are, but effectively it's just -- just further south of the previous drawing. The front line would have run --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would it help if you -- if you want to make a drawing on this? You think you can draw the front line on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: It's a little bit hard, but the front -- the front line was probably in front, sort of down behind -- running -- if you just go a centimetre above the top of the PTT building, you drew a line along there, if you took that down that would probably be roughly where the front line was, because the front line was roughly one block --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Why don't you take the electronic pen --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Have you just got the map that was here before?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe just on the photograph -- you can draw on the photograph the line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to remind you, and you've seen this a number of times from the other side, this isn't the PTT building. It is the Razvitak building which we've already seen on many previous photographs taken from the west. So this hit came from the east. Just to clarify matters straight away, and then it will be easier to discuss matters later on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. So draw an arrow there. So that line would then be continuing, so -- above that building?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: It's behind there, and it went in here somewhere, in between these buildings here. It's a bit hard on this drawing to actually, yeah, put it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you please put your signature here on a date, and if --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: This is taken from East Mostar, taken from the UNMO building, taken by myself with my camera in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can we get an IC number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will become IC 540.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Next photograph, 100003, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We can enlarge this a bit, but can you describe what's depicted here?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yeah. The -- I've just taken a shot of a -- of a mortar entering a property, which I recall was slightly south of the accommodation. The exact location I can't recall. It would have been in the -- I guess what is marked up on the map, the Brankovic or somewhere around there, but that's -- that's all it is, is a mortar going into a residential or -- sorry, I can't say it's a residential property because I can't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If we could then move to Exhibit 100004, please. Witness, what's depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That's the -- the road from the -- the west to the east, looking towards the Tito -- the entrance to the Tito Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is this taken from the west side or the east side of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That is from the west side. Can't -- can't remember exactly, but I would say probably around May. May or very early June, but it was before -- before we set up base.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just maybe to assist everyone here in the courtroom, if we can -- if you can put -- locate on the map on the ELMO the position where you -- from where you took this photograph.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, you've marked the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe we can get an IC number for this as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this map will become Exhibit IC 541.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please write your name down and sign it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's been done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, can you describe your daily tasks in your office at East Mostar? What was the daily -- your daily activities?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: They varied. The main -- in the early stages we were -- we were, of course, trying to enhance the cooperation between the BiH and the -- and the Croatian -- Bosnian Croatian forces or the HVO. We did regular patrols between the east and the west to talk to the various headquarters. We had established a liaison office with the -- with the HVO, and it was a Mr. Raguz, and we used to talk to Mr. Raguz or Blinka [phoen] Maric. And on the opposing side we would often talk to the local commander there who was Esad Husum [phoen] or -- sorry, I've forgotten his name, but it will ... Yeah, I haven't got that quite right, but anyway, so we would generally try and facilitate things such as the reconnection of water. We established communications with some difficulty. The difficulty there was, from memory, more from the armija side, but we -- we did get communications. However, they didn't last terribly long.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you say, "We established communications," communications with whom?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Between the -- our headquarters and the HVO. It was only a field telephone, so it was never going to be a great success with the amount of activity occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How long -- how long did -- this communication operated? How long did it function well?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Well, when it functioned we very rarely got answered, and then when it -- it probably only lasted two or three days before the wire was broke somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what were the type of things that you would be discussing with this HVO liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Well -- well, generally, I mean, the majority from the things from the team in East Mostar was obviously complaining about the main -- the targeting of the -- of our property and our vehicles. That -- that actually grew over time. I think initially the direct targeting of us probably wasn't that great. It seemed to grow over time. We were always trying to facilitate aid or -- or occasionally medical evacuations. Occasionally we arranged and the HVO allowed evacuation of, say, a seriously injured or ill child to their hospital which had the facilities. It -- nine times out of ten it was to try and -- the main concentration was to try and reduce the number of impacts on the population of East Mostar, which was primarily civilian but, obviously, also military.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What do you mean by "reduce the number of impacts on the population"?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Well, certainly, I mean, the -- the bombardment of East Mostar was not always heavy. It was extremely heavy after we turned -- when we moved in there on the -- whenever it was, the 5th of June. For a couple days there, there was a significant amount of impacts, primarily on the western side just immediately on the west of the Neretva River, which was only manned by military personnel, but also a significant number in the area between the main highway and the Neretva River on the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And was this also a military area?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: It was heavily populated with civilians that had been, as we mentioned earlier, relocated or forced over to the west side or whatever. They -- there were military -- there was military equipment that was being used in that area at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you to clarify something which you just said. You said, "It was heavily populated with civilians. It had been as we mentioned earlier relocated or forced over to the west side." Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yeah. What I'm saying there is -- is forced by either the trend of the fighting or they -- they kept coming over in the nights with reports that they were being forced across.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But forced across from where to where?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: From the -- the HVO occupied part of the town to -- into East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you give a bit of an indication on -- on the average number of shells that -- that fell in those first few days in June while you were there?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I believe in the first few days it was in the thousands. It -- I may be exaggerating here, but I seem to remember it was significantly high. But that was only for a couple of days and then it would be sporadic. It would possibly be -- range between 10, 12, 40 [sic] a day, maybe even down to one or two a day every so often. Yeah. And there were obviously some return fire. And, sorry, those -- those numbers are total.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said there was obviously some return fire. With what kind of weapons did the ABiH return their fire?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Well, the ABiH primarily had mortars, as I said earlier. That was their main what I would call artillery. And they had to be reasonably conservative with its use, as I understood. But certainly it was -- it was very one-sided if you're looking at the count of impacts on -- on one side. So there's obviously a lot more coming into the east side than was coming -- going into the west side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sometime earlier you've been referring to Muslim civilians being forced to cross over the confrontation line. Did you ever witness that yourself?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I can remember two occasions where I met up with what I would say, yeah, ones or twos, not people myself coming across having just been forced or allegedly forced over. However, my teams, particularly later in the piece, were able to certainly get more, have more contact with these types of people coming over. It was a frustrating period for us because there were the rumours coming around, but we -- we were unable to actually get to the position where -- where it was safe to actually observe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if I understand your answer correctly, you're saying that you got this information from people who actually crossed over, but you didn't see it yourself?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I didn't see it personally. My -- the team leader that took over or reopened the East Mostar office did -- was successful in actually witnessing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what is his name?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Pass. He was a Brit, British. He was a British UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, from the stories that you heard and from this -- this team leader that saw something, can you -- can you indicate, and again we still have the map on the ELMO, the areas where -- in Mostar where these Muslim civilians were being forced over the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Certainly the one -- I should actually clarify, but the Tito Bridge was one area where they actually did come across. In the earlier stages there were always -- we always got to see the people after the event, but there was always -- we will actually called it a bit of a body watch every morning. We'd look out around the Spanski Square area and just see if there were any more bodies out there. Quite often if they came in at night there were always -- well, not always, but that there were quite often stragglers or people that hadn't made it along that -- along the road that was in the last photo. So they were coming across the Tito Bridge, and I guess the bodies tend to support the fact that that was the route they were taking. The other thing -- the other area where they came, and I wouldn't be able to put my finger on where -- exactly where they were being put over, but we had a lot coming over the Donja Mahala area and over the -- originally over the Stari Grad bridge. And then later -- but they would be forced into the Donja Mahala area, but there was no room for them at the inn there, so they would make it across the Neretva River. And later on there was a temporary bridge put across there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you something to clarify about what you've just said. You've been talking about what you called a body watch that you -- you saw bodies at the Spanski Square. Was this in the month of June that you were -- that you were in the UNMO office that you saw these bodies?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the early stages of the conflict, and -- well, we -- probably actually through that month, actually, but it wasn't -- it wasn't every day. It was probably every third or fourth day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you give a number of the estimate of bodies that saw?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Not -- not a great number probably. Maybe a dozen over -- over the month. I'm very guarded with that figure, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: While you were in East Mostar in June 1993, were civilians ever being shot at by the -- by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: They were. Civilians were targeted regularly. We had a number of children hurt. We had a number of women, a number of old men. One of my -- one of my patrols had a child shot while the kids had stopped the UN vehicle to try and get lollies or whatever. So it was continual, the sniping on civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How did you get your information as to -- as to whether civilians were being shot in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Well, obviously my patrols. I'd see my guys out and do it and that's as -- as SMO and team leader in June. While I was in East Mostar I actually visited the hospital every night so I could keep track of who was getting hurt and how they were getting hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you report this information in -- in your UNMO reports?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I think we did most -- most of the time. I think probably quite tragically you tend to get a bit complacent, but I think that information was relayed in one form or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, just before the break I would like to show you another exhibit, Exhibit 2751. I can direct your -- you have to look in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: What number is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: 2751, please. If we look at page 2 of this report, under C it reads out: "Mostar relatively low-level fighting today with sporadic small-arms fire." MG, what does that stand for? Maybe you can read it and also give --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Okay. "Sporadic small-arms fire, machine-gun, anti-aircraft and mortar fire. A woman and child were killed by sniper fire in the east side of Mostar. UNMO seen."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would this be something that you would have reported? This is a report of the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That would probably be reported by myself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Having said that, I -- I didn't see that particular case. However, I do remember it well. A Danish UNMO, Soren Huson [phoen], and a Russian UNMO Oleg Gustav [phoen] were the ones that witnessed that and viewed the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I look at the clock. I don't know if it's time for a break or whether you want me to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now half past 5.00. We shall have a 20-minute break and resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing has resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Finlayson, during the period in June that you were in East Mostar, was your office in East Mostar ever targeted by HVO fire?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: It was never -- well, it wasn't targeted by artillery or mortar during my time in -- in East Mostar. Personnel and vehicles were often subjected to near misses with small-arms fire, which was most likely to be sniper fire from the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you ever targeted by sniping fire yourself?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I guess typically quite often there would tend to be around close by when we went up the stairs to our accommodation on -- I would say on rare occasion. You know, probably once -- once a week you'd -- you would probably say that you were nearly hit or whatever. One particular incident, I was -- and I'm not too sure whether it was -- when it was, but I was going down a road on the east side to -- from the Tito Bridge area, and the car was -- had probably around 15 rounds fired at it directly above my head for some instance, and then as the aim was adjusted a couple of rounds hit the -- at the rear of the car, underneath more or less, and then back up the top. I had absolutely no doubt that that particular time I was definitely the target and they were going for real. And that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who do you think was shooting at you at that time?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I believe due to the angle and where it was coming from it was coming from what we, I believe, term the bank building, which was occupied by the HVO. And another time was at the south end of town when a -- I was actually escorting General -- General -- in fact, he wasn't a general at the time. It was after his time as SMO, and he was working for Stoltenberg, but the past chief military observer, Bo Pellnas. And as we were exiting East Mostar, we were -- our vehicle received certainly one -- one hit and probably five, six, eight rounds. We took cover behind -- actually, I think it was an old railway wagon or something similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This particular incident that you just described, do you recall when this was?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: No. It must have been later in the piece. It must have been -- that one may have even been around either the end of 1993 or the beginning of 1994. I can't remember the date, sorry. But it was after -- it was after Bo's time as SMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just going back to that first incident that you described on the Tito Bridge, was that an incident that took place in -- in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I believe it was June 1993, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you ever reported complaints to your HVO liaison officer, Mr. Raguz, in relation to -- to the shooting -- to these shooting incidents?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Raguz probably got very sick of us reporting these incidents. They were always reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what would be the response of Mr. Raguz when you reported these incidents?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Raguz probably didn't give a lot of the responses. Most of the responses probably gave -- came from Mr. Maric, who would typically blame soldiers that were out of control or -- yeah, basically soldiers that were out of control that didn't agree with UNPROFOR's presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would the situation ever improve after having -- making complaints to Mr. Raguz or to Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit 2830, please. And in this document I would like to refer your attention to page 3, 4, and 5. And this is an incident report from an UNMO officer dated the 18th of June, 1993. Do you recall the particular incident that is described in this report?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Sorry, what paragraph am I reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No. Page 3 of this report.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just take a look at this report and tell us whether you recognise this incident.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I recall it well. They were very lucky to get away with that, to be alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell a bit more what happened here?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Essentially they were -- what we used to, in the quieter periods, travel for a period down the front line. Well, yeah, down the front line effectively across from west to east, and this patrol was coming from west to east, and it turned down an area where the front lines are basically across the street, and -- but it also turned a block. So the front line actually turned a 90 degree angle at that point. They turned down to head towards -- at 90 degrees to the road to the Tito Bridge before going over the Tito Bridge, and they received, I can't remember how many, but probably about seven rounds directly into the back of their patrol vehicle. It was a patrol clearly marked with "UN," and it received, I think from memory, five shots that luckily hit the rim of the spare tyre directly behind the driver, and another one went through slightly left and actually passed between the driver and the passenger, and a couple more went into the back of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if you flip of page of this -- of this report, you see that a drawing was made of the incident and then also a drawing of the back of the car on the next page. Now, based on this drawing, where would this fire that hit the UNMO vehicle would have come from?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Well, I think it's actually shown where the -- where it's got brackets to there, which is the position where I was firing, because the vehicle, it was directly behind the vehicle. There was no doubt of that due to the one that actually passed through the -- through the vehicle when dead straight down the middle of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And again, the area where it could have come from, under whose control would that area have been?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That was HVO at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, as a result of -- this incident resulted in a decision by the senior military observer in Mostar to withdraw the office -- the UNMO office from East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That's correct. I think it was really the nail in the coffin. I personally disagreed with the decision, but nevertheless, you do as you're told. It was the -- I -- yeah. It was the nail in the coffin, final nail in the coffin. The SMO made the decision that we'd probably lose someone before too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And why were you against this decision?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I think -- well, what actually I believe happened, I left the sector after we withdrew, but effectively the UN couldn't get back and there for a short time, I believe. Just having a presence there, being able to report what was happening, I think my impression was that it was keeping -- keeping things at bay a little bit. Otherwise, the situation may have deteriorated with no reports going out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you've said you left the sector. Where did you go and how long did you leave for?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I left for Kiseljak. I became the -- the UNMO operations officer in the Kiseljak -- in the BH command headquarters. I was up there for, I guess, around three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what were your duties in those three months, just in a few words?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Effectively we -- we worked very much as a team there but we were concerned about the overall situation in Bosnia, full stop. If -- depending on -- on -- what was happening really depended on what operations we were working on. We'd spend a bit of time up Mount Igman with operations happening there between the Serbs and the -- and the armija. We also spent a lot of time in Fojnica, around that area, which at that particular time was -- was active. I also think we -- the Maglaj pocket or at that stage it was a finger, it became a pocket, was also sort of happening at that time, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you've said you spent some time at the Mount Igman. Did you ever -- visited Sarajevo this, these three months?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yeah, regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Regularly. Now, is it correct that you returned to the Mostar area on the 21st of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That is correct. As -- I returned as the senior military observer at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So at that time you were the senior military observer of -- of the BH South on --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, having spent some time in Sarajevo as well, and having -- coming -- coming back to the area of Mostar, can you tell the Court, looking at the situation in Mostar and comparing it to the situation in the town of Sarajevo, how would you compare these two situations?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Sarajevo was under siege as -- as East Mostar was. It was lucky to have a high presence of international bodies and a high media presence. Of course the later can be -- can go either ways, but the mere fact that there was a high media presence there meant that things were kept at -- at bay a little bit. Mostar didn't have that. The condition, the fear -- sorry. The conditions for the people on west side was probably better than in Sarajevo. However, the people on the east side, due to the sheer number in such a small area, was worth -- was worse both in the humanitarian side, in food side, and -- and because a condensed area and the number of impacts. And when I say the number of impacts compared with -- with Sarajevo, the per metre -- I know I looked at it a couple of times and I can't recall the figure, but the number of times per square kilometre, rather, rounds per day or whatever was -- was significantly more over much of the time in Mostar. And of course the problem was that the -- the media wasn't allowed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you returned to Mostar in -- on the 21st of September, 1993, was there an UNMO office in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes. It had been reopened at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And was there also an office in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I believe it -- yeah. I was -- I was racking my brains on whether it was set up just after I arrived or -- I think it was just after I arrived we set up a -- an office in West Mostar. That -- I mean, that was invaluable because it gave us better representation on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, earlier when we spoke about the period of June, about Muslim civilians being forced by the HVO to cross the confrontation line into East Mostar, had this practice stopped in September 1993 when you returned?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: No. I -- no, it hadn't. And in fact, that's when I -- I mentioned that the British UNMO actually got in a position where he could see it and did quite a comprehensive report at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So that was --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That was -- that would have been in September or October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at Exhibit 5519, please. And if I can direct your attention to page 3 of this report. And look on the top of the page. I'll read it out, the second part of the paragraph. "HVO released 374 civilians, old men, women and children from West Mostar to East Mostar. HVO opened fire on these people, killing -- killing two. UNMOs visited these peoples in refugee camp, report that they are in very bad condition." Is this the situation you just referred to with the British UNMO officer reporting on expulsions? This is a report dated the 30th of September. Let me ask you, do you recall this -- this particular report?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I don't recall it, that particular report. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We can move then to Exhibit 5553, which is a report dated the 1st of October, 1993, and I can direct your attention to page number 5. And under paragraph 8, and I'll read it out again: "Two truckloads of refugees were expelled by HVO across confrontation line from Buna towards Blagaj today. Reportedly these refugees were from Capljina and Dretelj. Reference yesterday's sitrep expelling of refugees across the confrontation line by HVO is very often incident. There are numerous -- there are numbers of body lying in no man's land. UNMOs on ground faces difficulties in recognising the bodies as to which are fresh or a month old." Can you comment on this report?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I recall the incident vaguely, but I -- no. No. I think it would be safer to say no on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to be -- to interrupt, but I assume that the gentleman was shown these reports and would have given these answers to the Prosecution prior to bringing the witness to go over reports which he now tells us that, you know, he doesn't recall. So perhaps he could just go through the reports that the gentleman has assured him he can testify about at the proofing session rather than reading matters from the report into the record hoping to get something from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Witness, let me -- let me ask you. As a senior military officer, as a senior military officer in -- in the BH South region, would reports coming from areas like Mostar, would these reports have come to you, and would you have seen them at the -- at the time?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I would have, and that's why I'm a little bit bemused by this one. But most reports went via me, but of course there were other -- there were times because I was controlling the entire south -- southern area, there were times when they -- they wouldn't necessarily pass across me if I wasn't at the -- at the Medjugorje office. As I say, I -- I recall the incident but I can't provide information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, do you recall participating in a -- in a cease-fire meeting for the Mostar area around early October 1993? And this was a meeting which involved SpaBat and UN CIVPOL, Mr. Albert Benabou.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what do you recall about this meeting? If it's -- if it's helpful to you, let me show you an exhibit to you Exhibit 5553?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Have a look at Exhibit 5553. My apologies, yes. If you can move to page number 4, please. And if you can read paragraph 4, which starting: "The highlight of the CMO's days was attending the cease-fire meeting between the BiH and the HVO chaired by Albert Benabou at SpaBat." Do you read that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I recall the meeting. I think the outcome was as I've alluded to there is probably typical. We always had the problem of dealing with two areas, one where the HVO was in control and one where the armija were in control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he just indicated previously that he didn't recognise this document. Now he's talking about alluding to something in the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So did the gentleman generate this document? And if he's going to be refreshed, his memory, I think a more proper way to do so might be by pointing him to areas in his notebook, because his notebook are based on notes that he took to meetings that he attended, and that might be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This -- can I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You know, we have a procedure here. Nobody is trying to stifle your creativity on the stand. Now, I would like an answer. Did the gentleman generate this document? If not, then he shouldn't be making a reference that he's alluding to passages that he -- he wasn't the author. If he is the author then that's the foundation then he can comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say and reply to that that I probably was the author of that particular paragraph. This is a report that has been generated at UNMO BH command, so it would not have been drafted. Sorry, this particular document wouldn't have been drafted in BH but segments -- BH South, rather, but segments of it would have been, and effectively cut and pasted to make the BH command report. If you recall the sequence I explained early on with the chain of command. So this, this segment of my meeting, was most likely reported by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall who represented the HVO and the ABiH at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I believe Berko Pusic may have been at this one. The armija. I can't recall. Possibly Pasalic, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You mention a person named Berko Pusic. Who is Mr. Berko Pusic? What was his function?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: He had a range -- at one stage in the early pieces he was assigned as the liaison person, from memory. This was the case very much in my earlier days in BH South. I think his role as -- as liaison remained but with a presence in East Mostar a lot of that was taken over by Mr. Raguz as the direct contact. He -- I'm struggling to -- to get the correct term that we understood him to -- to have, but it was I think to do with misplaced people. I -- yeah. I -- probably it will come to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What kind of dealings did the UNMO have with Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: We had quite a bit to do with Mr. Pusic. We generally -- quite often when we were stuck or things were not going quite as they were meant to be, Mr. Pusic had an uncanny way of turning up, and generally we used to joke about it, but once he came into the equation we could guarantee we wouldn't get any further. He dealt a lot with the body exchanges. With -- at that point most of the body exchanges were happening between -- well, at the early stages most of the body exchanges were past ones with the Serbs, but then, of course, later on as the Mostar situation developed it -- we also had both body exchanges and prisoner exchanges with -- between the east and west.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said Mr. Pusic had an uncanny way of turning up. Where would he turn up? Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: If we were stuck somewhere and ranting and raving, trying to get access to, for instance, Mostar, I can remember very clearly one day I had a message to deliver, and it may not have been the same day that a Spanish soldier had been killed, and we wanted access to, number one, deliver the message; number two, deliver assistance to the Spanish soldier. And at that stage the UNMO as well as the Spanish ambulance or -- sorry, medical APC or whatever, was held up at the check-point to Mostar and wasn't allowed in. And that was one instance where I clearly remember Mr. Pusic as -- as being the spokesman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall when this -- around what time this happened?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: No. I'd need jogging on that one. It would have been -- it may have been around June, July. No, it can't have been July. June.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's turn back to the meeting, Mr. Finlayson. Let me draw your attention to Exhibit -- two more exhibits on this meeting. Exhibit 5567. If I can draw your attention to page number 3. And this is an UNMO report dated the 2nd of October. Now, on the paragraph 3, and I'll read it and ask you some questions about it. "Meeting continued between HVO and BiH delegations at SpaBat. The memorandum signed at the end of the day covers the protection of civil population covering locations of hospitals, shelling, sniping of civilian targets, et cetera. During the course of the day the primary paragraph concerning cease-fire was deleted. This was primarily due to the HVO opposition to this in such a localised area and would not have signed the document." Now, can you -- let me first ask you, were you the one who reported -- reported this particular paragraph?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what do you mean when you said this was -- to this -- that this was primarily due to the HVO operation to this in such a localised area? Can you explain what you meant by this?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I think I may have alluded to it earlier that within -- within the BH South area there were -- there was the northern range -- region, part of it, that was controlled by the armija, and on the southern side it was obviously the -- the HVO were really in the controlling seat. So the HVO's opposition was merely to the effect where they believed that we were concentrating on -- on -- on Mostar and the UN wasn't doing the same in the northern area where they were in the -- in the weaker position. So they -- I guess they thought there was an unbalance there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If we can now move to Exhibit 5571. You see this is an UNPROFOR civil affairs document which actually attaches the text of the memorandum that was signed as a result of this -- of this meeting. And if I could ask you first maybe to move to the last page, to the signators. That is page 4 of the document. It says here Mr. Berislav Pusic for the HVO. Now you've been referring to Berko Pusic. Would this have been the same person?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I believe -- I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who signed the document on behalf of the BiH?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pusic, Berislav.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, for the BiH?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: For the BiH? Alija Alikadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of questions on the content of this memorandum, and if I could ask you to go to part number 2 which reads "Protection of civilian populations." Now, under 1A it reads the following: "The parties pledge to take special efforts to protect the civil population throughout Mostar --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel please slow down when they read, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: "The parties pledge to take special efforts to protect civilian population throughout Mostar. In particular, the following steps shall be taken: "A. Military installations shall be situated at a reasonable distance from the hospitals, apartments, buildings, other dwellings and public areas." Why was this paragraph included in the memorandum?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I believe it was included because of the HVO's insistence that the BiH were firing from the vicinity of the hospital in east -- East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And was this in fact the case? Did this happen?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I believe on -- in cases it was confirmed by -- I know I confirmed it at least once myself, and my team over the next year probably would have confirmed it three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what kind of action did you undertake when such a situation --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Well, just reversed roles, really. We'd go to the -- the headquarters of the armija in East Mostar and get them to shift it and try and monitor it as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if you asked them to shift it, would they -- would they actually do that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: They would. But on occasion it would find its way back there or to another similar place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to paragraph number 3. "In accordance with the provisions of Article 3 of the IV Geneva Convention, no violence to life or outrages upon personal dignity of people, including their expulsion from their home or territory, shall be perpetrated." Why was this paragraph included?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: That would have been as a direct result of the -- the expulsions or the flow of people from the west to east that was being enforced by the HVO and also the -- I guess it also covers the sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. That's it for the document. Mr. Finlayson, do you recall ever visiting -- in October ever visiting the Donja Mahala area in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I did, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what can you recall about this visit?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Essentially I -- I actually went over there to -- to investigate the claims of an aerial bombardment. I'm not too sure, but they certainly had a fairly large explosion in one area. However, we also went along. They also reported the rolling of tyres filled with explosives down the hill, which was immediately behind the area, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of that hill?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: We always referred to it as the -- the Hum. Hum, H-u-m, I think, if I remember. And so, I mean, that was confirm as much as we confirmed. There were signs of -- of tyres that had -- both exploded and unexploded tyres. The armija had put up a makeshift fence to stop these things hitting the accommodation blocks where the people were -- were living.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And based on what you saw, would you agree that -- that these tyres actually had -- had been rolling from the hills? What was your conclusion as to this investigation?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: I -- I actually did conclude that they -- it looked like they had been done, certainly the type of damage in the location and the surrounding evidence. I don't think it was necessary a great success, but it certainly did some significant damage to lower floor of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, as a senior military observer in the region, did you ever make complaints to the HVO authority as -- on things that were reported to you by -- by UNMO observers under your supervision?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: We did. Again, because I was involved in the broader side of it, quite often I'd delegate that to either my deputy or -- or sometimes just senior competent members, but all -- all reports that we confirmed were taken up with the -- the authorities at the local level in general, and I guess the -- the scheme of attack was that all these reports going via Kiseljak and Zagreb would -- would prompt, as I knew it did from my time in the headquarters, would prompt discussions even at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, at your level, if you would raise the complaints at your level, to who would you complain?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: It varied, I guess, on who was there and the incident. I made a lot of complaints. I still used my retrofit. Occasionally we would, if it was significant or if we got direction from the higher powers to maybe make a point of it, we would do it to General Petkovic in Citluk or I -- later we -- we went over to Posusje to -- with General Roso.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just for the purposes of the transcript it didn't pick up the place where you would have -- you said General Petkovic in --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Citluk. And what was in Citluk?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: It was where his headquarters was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how would you make these complaints, verbally or in writing?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: General -- generally, and verbally I think on a couple of occasions and it would probably only be a couple of occasions we would have penned a letter, and that would have been typically after discussions with the high headquarters that maybe they wanted to just, you know, put something in writing, black and white.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall anything about the content of the complaint that you would have raised with General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON
utterances.text: Well, generally the tipped attacks on UNMO and civilian population. That was a -- general, run of the mill complaints we have. We had various occasions where UNMO vehicles were detained maybe ransacked or whatever, and most of those went in writing if they had interfered with the UNMO vehicle directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see Ms. Alaburic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I apologise to my learned friend for interrupting as well, but I think we must be more specific about this issue. When were those objections raised, and what specific events were those in relation to, the complaints? Because this general question can relate to any complaints at all, and we must know when this occurred in order to know what position General Petkovic was holding at that time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you've heard the Defence question, and I'll ask again. Can you think of a specific incident where you went to General Petkovic and complained about the incident?
